key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the evidence of P.W.1 and P.W.2, who testified that the appellant shot the deceased, and the material objects recovered from the scene of crime, including a country-made pistol and an empty cartridge, which were identified by the appellant.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, noting that their depositions corroborated the materials recovered from the scene of crime and the FIR, and that the presence of the other accused with weapons was not proved.
post_offence_conduct: The appellant has undergone the sentence for a period of 13 years 6 months and 20 days without remission and has good conduct during this period.
custody_duration: 13 years 6 months and 20 days without remission and the total sentence of 17 years 1 month and 9 days
bail_history: Appellant was released on bail by the Supreme Court on 27.01.2020
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 30.10.1997; Trial judgment: 16.05.2006; High Court decision: 16.12.2011; Supreme Court decision: 14 October 2024
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Mrs. Sudha Gupta, R.S. Rathi, Ms. Kusum; Counsel for the State: Akshat Kumar, Ms. Anubha Dhulia
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction and sentence affirmed; High Court: Dismissed appeal and affirmed judgment; Supreme Court: Partly allowed appeal
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant shot the deceased, and the charge of murder framed against him was proved beyond doubt. The evidence of P.W.1 and P.W.2, along with material objects recovered from the scene, supported the prosecution's case.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution's case was inconsistent and lacked sufficient evidence to prove the appellant's involvement beyond reasonable doubt. They also claimed that the appellant should be acquitted due to the acquittal of the other accused and the lack of proof of premeditation.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that even with minor discrepancies in the evidence, the prosecution's case can still be sustained if the core facts are established. It also emphasized the principle of proportionality in sentencing.
precedent_relied_upon: C. Muniappan v. State of Tamil Nadu [2010] 10 SCR 262 : (2010) 9 SCC 567; Shiva Kumar @ Shiva @ Shivamurthy v. State of Karnataka [2023] 4 SCR 669 : (2023) 9 SCC 817; Navas @ Mulanavas v. State of Kerala [2024] 3 SCR 913 : 2024 SCC OnLine SC 315; Union of India v. V. Sriharan [2015] 14 SCR 613 : (2016) 7 SCC 1
sentencing_rationale: The sentence was modified to the period already undergone by the appellant due to the lack of premeditation, his good conduct during incarceration, and the possibility of reformation.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The appellant's good conduct during incarceration, his poor economic background, and the possibility of reformation were considered as mitigating factors.
judicial_aggravating_factors: The aggravating factors included the sudden provocation, the use of a weapon, and the fact that the victim died due to gunshot injuries.
other_sentence_order: The appellant was required to pay the fine amount imposed by the Sessions Court if not already paid. The bail bond executed by the appellant was discharged.
